I think almost everything about my $AXTI thesis from 2025 was validated? 

From AXT's position in the InP substrate bottleneck... Being able to threaten the hyperscaler buildout (per Reuters)... 

$IQE has been flagging this as a major risk, VPEC and Taiwan epiwafer foundries have been crying over InP substrate bottlenecks.

Now... the biggest question is: How much can AXT price hike? 

The substrates they make are just such a tiny part of the BOM... but can threaten hyperscaler buildouts with optics. 

So if they manage to price hike to $SNDK NAND degrees (which they can), then I think AXT could get re-rated a ton from here. But if they end up like Japanese ABF suppliers that are less willing to abuse their position, that's a different story.  

Will need to do more channel checks to see how that's coming along.

But at the very least, I would argue there should be some valuation baseline just due to their critical importance (eg. upstream refinery ownerships, crucible processing, etc) + existing capacity revenue without hikes. 

TLDR: 
- Bottleneck thesis was at like ~$500m MC 
- Upside now comes from price hikes due to duopoly position + ownership of upstream bottlenecks in the InP substrate manufacturing process. (which they can due to low cost of InP substrates in overall costs) 
- Uncharted territory, we'll see (also a central part of geopolitical tensions so there's always risk there).

Shocking stat of the day:

$241 billion worth of French corporate bonds are now trading at lower yields than French government bonds.

This figure is up +1,621% from just $14 billion at the start of 2026.

This means ~38% of French high-grade corporate debt is now trading at lower yields than government bonds of similar maturity.

The gap between corporate and government bond yields is widening as investor concerns about France's deteriorating fiscal situation weigh on government debt.

As a result, internationally exposed companies such as L'Oreal, $OR, and TotalEnergies, $TTE, are increasingly viewed as safer alternatives to French government debt, unlike French banks, which remain more exposed to sovereign risk.

This is in stark contrast to normal economic conditions, when government bonds are traditionally viewed as the safest part of the bond market.

France's corporate bond market is increasingly being treated a safer bet than its government bonds.

Good question! Just some informal thoughts... there's three "moats" to look at for $SIVE:

- Capacity 
- Qualifications (especially for custom DFB lasers)
- Technological

1. For capacity, they're coming online with 100M+ CW DFB lasers Q4 2027 (global supply is roughly ~608M EML/CW lasers currently per Trendforce). 

Obviously by 2027 global capacity is going to grow a lot, with $AAOI, $AVGO (3x expansion), and others coming online.  

But if you extrapolate their 2:1 statement, that implies 300m lasers/year long term coming from their own supply + external foundries. 

This is incredibly valuable during a shortage that was quoted to be 3-5 years, and $LITE stating they already have demand visibility into 2031...

And when suppliers have started to qualify many more (eg. 5-7 vendors vs. 2-3 earlier) due to bottlenecks. 

I'm sure a lot of how they achieve that staggering amount is due to their manufacturing process/yields (which is a moat). 

2. For qualifications, if you look at 70mW/100mW pluggable lines with Chinese players, I'd argue this is more generic and moreso reverting back to a capacity  argument and manufacturing process to achieve those numbers. 

Custom DFB arrays that they've been working on with Ayar (they hinted at 2-3 others back in 2023 like Celestial) take years for optical i/o related things and would be a moat if they finish quals. 

So it's not quite something you can hot swap or design out really easily for $MTSI or another company. But of course cpo scale up and such is mass volume in 2028, and we're still H2 2026. 

3. People can always compare raw specs like power output, but it's probably way way more nuanced so easier to just point toward customer statements. 

With $JBL 1.6T LRO: "I think that there's the potential for a relatively dramatic moat with our LRO part…" from Jabil's EVP, especially related to power consumption. And $SIVE is my guess sole source in this line. 

Jabil is probably the most important testament to how their lasers perform in mass production scenarios maybe around Q2 next year.

How do you know when to sell? 

Here are 4 different sell rules 👇

1️⃣ Sell strength
Don't wait for the top. When a stock is running in your favor, take some off into the move.

2️⃣ Sell when it doesn't hold above a prior high
If a stock pushes through the old high and then slips back under it, the buyers didn't follow through. That's your cue to reduce.

3️⃣ Sell when it goes red
A trade that was working and flips from green to red is telling you something. Don't let a winner turn into a loser while you hope it comes back.

4️⃣ Sell when the trade really changes and gets below a prior day's low
The prior day's low is the line in the sand. Once price breaks below it, the character of the trade has changed. Respect it and step aside.

You don't need one perfect exit. You need rules you set before you're in the trade.

On me demande souvent si je suis croyant. La réponse honnête, c'est que je suis agnostique. Mais pas un agnostique tiède, qui hausse les épaules et passe à autre chose. Un agnostique entièrement tourné vers une seule obsession : chercher la vérité et comprendre l'univers.

Ça repose sur quelques convictions simples.

D'abord, il existe une vérité, et elle mérite qu'on lui consacre sa vie. Je ne prétends pas la posséder. Je prétends la chercher. Pour ça, je n'ai pas trouvé de meilleure méthode que celle de Socrate : questionner sans relâche, à commencer par ses propres certitudes. Savoir qu'on ne sait pas, c'est le point de départ de toute vraie connaissance. Celui qui a déjà toutes les réponses, qu'il soit dogmatique religieux ou matérialiste intégriste, a arrêté de penser.

Ensuite, il y a de la vérité dans tout, et là où il y a de la vérité, la beauté émerge. Je crois profondément qu'une forme de beauté objective existe. Le visage d'une belle femme, une symphonie qui sonne juste, une équation élégante, une cathédrale, un coucher de soleil sur la côte bretonne. Ce n'est pas qu'une question de goût. Quand quelque chose est vrai, harmonieux, bien construit, presque tout le monde le reconnaît. La beauté est le signal que l'on touche à quelque chose de juste.

Cela implique de refuser la laideur. Pas par snobisme, mais par exigence. On s'est habitués à vivre entourés de choses moches : une architecture sans âme, des objets jetables, des systèmes absurdes. Je pense qu'une civilisation saine doit construire des systèmes qui tendent vers la beauté. Et la bonne nouvelle, c'est qu'il existe une infinité de beautés possibles. On n'a pas fini d'en créer.

Cette beauté ne s'arrête pas aux formes, elle existe aussi dans les idées. Une idée vraie a souvent quelque chose d'élégant. C'est pour ça que je trouve les idées économiques fondées sur la liberté si convaincantes, de l'école autrichienne de Hayek et Mises jusqu'à Milton Friedman. Elles partent d'un principe simple : des individus libres, qui échangent librement, créent spontanément un ordre que personne n'aurait pu planifier. Il y a là une beauté d'horloger. Et à mes yeux, il n'y a rien de plus beau que la liberté individuelle.

Enfin, le sens de tout ça, c'est le dépassement de soi. Chercher la vérité, créer de la beauté, défendre la liberté, ce sont trois façons de dire la même chose : devenir plus grand que ce qu'on est aujourd'hui.

C'est pour ça que je me sens si en phase avec le projet d'Elon Musk. Au fond, son projet n'est ni technologique ni commercial. C'est un projet de dépassement. Il s'agit de continuer à jouer le jeu, de repousser la frontière, de découvrir ce qu'il y a derrière.

Je n'ai pas besoin d'un dogme pour donner un sens à ma vie. J'ai besoin d'une direction. La mienne tient en une phrase : chercher la vérité, tendre vers la beauté, et comprendre l'univers tant qu'il reste quelque chose à comprendre.

posts.text:
Waymo and Zoox first impressions

I use self driving on my Tesla all the time, but I finally got around to trying the commercial autonomous ride hailing services this week in Las Vegas.

The biggest issue by far is the very limited pickup and dropoff points, and only having a couple minutes to get to them resulted in a bit of a rush.

If you are going to have a small-integer number of locations, you should make it super-obvious where those locations are. Waymo included a picture, but it was a rather undistinguished parking garage image and it wasn’t clear which floor it was on. Being able to switch the map to an aerial photography view might be helpful in some cases. Pan-able 360 photos of the target points might also be helpful.

The first Zoox ride was flawless, but we had a lengthy walk to get to our actual destination.

The first Waymo ride was a little rougher. It felt more indecisive with steering, like Teslas did a couple years ago. This was still early-access in Vegas, so it is probably better in the active commercial markets.

The second Zoox ride had a small incident – there was another Zoox ahead of us at a stoplight (and a Waymo and another Zoox next to us!) that repeatedly tried to back up into our Zoox, to the point that ours actually honked at the one ahead of it a couple times. Eventually, after multiple light cycles, ours started to tentatively try to get around it, which left it partway into the next lane and distressingly close to a fast moving semi. The one ahead finally moved, and the ride continued normally.

Overall, the Zoox experience felt a bit more charming than the Waymo, with several nice little touches, but they both get the job done. I still need to try a Cybercab.

Isaiah, after everything we’ve been through together I’m surprised that you would publicize our disagreement in this fashion. But since you have created public interest in this, it is important that people should hear both sides of the story.

Day One has been a major investor in Valar from the beginning, and we have never wavered in our belief that the company will be a success. This faith and support in our founders is why fourteen Day One founders have become limited partners in Day One’s most recent fund.

In 2024, Day One invested in Valar’s seed round. Later that year, Valar required a seed extension after miscalculations by management regarding the capital needs of the business. Day One stepped in to provide this seed extension, saving the company in a difficult time.

When it came time to raise a Series A, Valar spent several weeks on the market without success. At Valar’s request, Day One then offered the first term sheet and co-led the Series A, again saving the company during a time when deep tech startups in highly regulated industries were a difficult sell in venture capital.

Then when Valar needed a Series A extension, Isaiah asked that Day One waive our pro rata rights so as to make a tenuous financing deal work out. We agreed for the good of the company.

As part of these transactions, Valar agreed that, if their long-shot effort to build nuclear energy as a startup did succeed, Day One would have rights to participate in future rounds that could not be eliminated without Day One’s consent. This was a fair bargain at a time when Day One took extraordinary risks by betting against the market when Valar’s future appeared highly uncertain. Following the achievement of criticality on June 18th, our faith has been validated. Valar went from being an obscure company to a hot startup. We congratulate the Valar team on their hard won success!

Of course, when it came time for Valar to raise a Series B after achieving such success, Day One expected to participate in that round – as both parties had agreed. But at this point the normally positive communications between Day One and Valar took a negative turn. Valar insisted that Day One give up all of its future pro rata rights despite the parties’ agreements, and despite four out of six major investors participating in the Series B round without waiving. This went against both the letter and the spirit of our deal, so we did not agree. In decades of investing we have waived pro-rata rights dozens of times, but no other company has ever demanded that we give up all of our rights for all future rounds.

We told Isaiah we would give up a majority of our pro-rata in the Series B round so as to not make his life difficult, to which he responded “You cannot make my life difficult, I can make your life difficult.”  It was at this point that we sought representation with Quinn Emanuel to protect the firm and the interests of our limited partners.

Day One has since learned of a significant secondary equity sale by Isaiah from which we were excluded. Our attempts to gain insights into this through our information rights have been stymied by Valar management, who have refused to produce material documents requested by Day One. After weeks of delay on these documents, Valar management alerted us this Wednesday that they intend to pursue legal action against Day One unless we waive our legal rights forever.

We have always pursued positive and mutually beneficial relationships with all of our portfolio companies. We have neither taken nor threatened legal action against Valar, and in fact we told them explicitly that we have no interest in doing so. Valar voluntarily entered into a contract with Day One, then violated that contract, and is now suing Day One. 

We are deeply disappointed by this recent erratic turn, but are still proud of our early and continued support of Valar.  We look forward to the clarity from the courts that Valar’s management is seeking.

posts.name: Patrick Collison
posts.text:
Assorted things I've been mulling over regarding agents in the economy:

• Companies are in some sense the original superintelligence. It's often the case that they can use their amortized cognitive surplus to advance their interests against those of certain consumers: relative to the optimization capacity of companies, consumers can be inattentive, underinformed, irrational, etc. (Think, say, of some of the classic insurance upsells at the end of a booking process, which is typically priced substantially above what a regular policy would cost.) Herbert Simon introduced the idea of bounded rationality, and firms often end up benefiting from it. Thanks to personal agents, we will probably get somewhat more rational in how we engage with companies.

• How exactly will outcomes change? Well, certain kinds of price discrimination will work less well (how do coupons work if every agent hunts fastidiously for them?), and certain kinds of customer cross-subsidy will change (today, people who forget to cancel subscriptions subsidize those who don't). Taken across the economy as a whole, I'm not sure what the incidence of all of this will be.

• In corporate strategy, people have long debated the relative importance of distribution and product quality. Perhaps you've made something better, but does anyone know about it? Won't people just continue to buy the ACME Corp Mousetraps? Personal agents will, I think, act as a kind of structural subsidy for product quality. How would markets look different if individuals always spent at least 10 hours researching their purchases? On the margin, focusing on making a product better is, I think, going to become a more effective strategy for companies. This is good!

• It true, a corollary is that information about product quality will become more important and impactful. Today, most people have very limited ability to aggregate and integrate such data, but agents will have insatiable thirst for such signals. (It's often said that data is becoming more valuable because it helps in the training of models. That's obviously true, but I think there's a secondary way in which it's more valuable simply as a complement to cheaper intelligence.)

• A big question is whether agents will increase superstar effects (rational agents all settle on the same product) or increase dispersion (because everyone has slightly different tastes and preferences, which agents are good at eliciting, finally overcoming the artificial clustering we've been subjected to).

• Many internet companies have monetized demand routing, which is in turn often predicated on short attention spans. "I'll click on the first thing I see." This has led to some amount of inefficiency, as companies try to propitiate capricious ranking algorithms and incur various placement fees. It's not all deadweight loss (willingness to pay is itself a kind of signal, which is valuable to buyers), but it's not great. How will the nature and value of this routing change in a world of personal agents? I don't know the answer, but I think that the effects might be pretty big.

• Much of what I'm writing hinges on the assumption that personal agents will be on the consumer's side. I suspect that that will be the winning strategy, but whether it's true, and what it means to be true, involves a lot of other questions.

Taken as a whole, the market is a massively parallelized, decentralized, and highly imperfect value attribution machine, and, taking stock of all of the effects, it seems to me that the quality point may well be the biggest: that agents will change the nature of the backpropagation such that the rewards for better products increase. Maybe this is too optimistic, but I suspect (and hope) that companies that make things that they're proud of will feel that the universe is a little more partisan in their favor.

posts.text:
T-Mobile CTO in new post on @SpaceX acquiring nationwide low-band spectrum to help turn Starlink into a major U.S. mobile carrier:

"Some are calling it the "last critical piece" needed to compete with the national wireless carriers. I can tell you there's a big difference between owning spectrum and delivering a great mobile experience to millions of customers.

A few things worth keeping in perspective:

1) Spectrum is just the starting point. 
The Grain transaction involves approximately 14 MHz of spectrum that T-Mobile previously divested because it was no longer central to our network strategy. Even with this acquisition, @Starlink Mobile would have roughly 80 MHz of spectrum, some of it uplink-only. Compare that to T-Mobile's nearly 400 MHz of mid-band and low-band spectrum holdings.

We used 800 MHz spectrum as a single 5 MHz uplink/5 MHz downlink channel for LTE years ago. Today, we're operating a nationwide 5G Standalone network, launched nationwide 5G-Advanced, and are already helping shape the path to 6G, all using channels that are much wider. The industry has moved forward and so have the expectations of customers. 

2) Physics still applies. 
A satellite hundreds of kilometers above Earth faces approximately 50 dB more path loss than a terrestrial cell site just a kilometer away. Moving from 2 GHz to 800 MHz recovers only a few dB of that enormous disadvantage. 

Lower-frequency spectrum can help improve satellite connectivity, but it doesn't change the fundamental physics. A satellite signal traveling hundreds of kilometers simply faces challenges that a nearby cell tower doesn't.

3) Indoor coverage is where the real test begins. 
More than 70% of mobile traffic takes place indoors. Think about where you use your phone most: at home, in the office, inside a store, or at a crowded venue. 

That's where terrestrial networks have a fundamental advantage. Buildings, walls, and other obstacles make it much harder for signals traveling from space to reach customers reliably. Direct-to-Cell technology can extend connectivity to outdoor places traditional networks don't reach, but delivering a consistent indoor mobile experience is a very different challenge. 

4) Capacity matters just as much as coverage. 
One satellite beam can cover an area served by hundreds of terrestrial cell sectors. Those terrestrial sectors provide the network density needed to support millions of customers streaming video, making calls, working, gaming, and using data simultaneously. 

Covering a geographic area is one thing. Delivering the speed, responsiveness, and capacity customers expect from a modern 5G-Advanced network is another. 

Direct-to-Cell has an important role to play in extending coverage. But it is a complement to terrestrial networks, not a replacement for the capacity of a dense 5G-Advanced network. 

5) Building a great network takes more than capital. It takes time and experience. 
The U.S. wireless industry has invested more than $250B in network infrastructure since 2018. That’s on top of more than $200B in spectrum auctions over the past decade, plus the stores, care, and distribution that support customers every day.  And that investment represents only part of what it takes to deliver a great wireless experience.

You can acquire spectrum in a single transaction. You cannot acquire a nationwide, high-performing wireless network overnight.

If this is truly the beginning of a new wireless provider in America, we welcome competition. It's good for innovation, good for the industry, and most importantly, good for customers.

But great wireless networks aren't built with headlines or spectrum licenses alone. They're built site by site, neighborhood by neighborhood, in subway tunnels, office buildings, stadiums, and communities across America.

Spectrum is an essential ingredient. But it takes a network to deliver on its promise."

Someone at ABC owes the public an answer. “No comment” will not hold.

This story might be a little “inside baseball” for those outside media and journalism but it is causing a stir inside the industry. It’s the mystery over ABC News publishing a story on Wednesday morning it which it claimed defense companies backed by the President’s sons have raked in more than $6 billion in active or promised government contracts since those investments were made — and then taking the story down in a day with no explanation.

It’s a big deal because the it got a lot of attention when it went live Wednesday. ABC promoted it on X with a graphic: “President Trump’s sons’ investments have won billions in Pentagon contracts since his election.” It was shared by lawmakers and Democratic officials, per CNN’s Andrew Kaczynski. Gavin Newsom put it in front of 900,000 people and wrote that “accountability is coming.”

Forbes, citing an anonymous source, reports the story was removed after being “published prematurely.” CNN’s Brian Stelter, who was also told that, called it obviously not a sufficient explanation.

Palmer Luckey, whose company Anduril is at the center of the story, claims he contacted ABC after the story went live on Wednesday morning and that he demanded a correction. "After multiple rounds of refusal, they finally make a single one-word grammar edit.  The editors stand by the reporting and insist the false claims are true.  Finally, eight hours after I was forced to call them out publicly, they delete everything."

If that account is accurate, “published prematurely” is hard to square with editors who stood by the story for hours. Luckey also alleges the story was a coordinated influence operation planted by competitors. He has offered no evidence I’ve seen, and I am not repeating that as fact.

But take Luckey out of it entirely. ABC still has a problem it cannot solve with silence. Either the story was wrong, in which case readers deserve to be told what was wrong, or it was right, in which case it should not have vanished. ABC can resolve this in one paragraph. The one option that is not acceptable is saying nothing.

ABC knows what accountability looks like. In 2017, after a botched Michael Flynn report, it apologized publicly, said the story hadn’t been properly vetted, and suspended their top investigative reporter, Brian Ross, for four weeks without pay. Nobody is asking for that here. What is being asked for is one on-the-record statement.

The Trump sons’ business dealings are fair game, and if they profited from government contracts, that is a legitimate story. That is exactly why this matters. A story erased without explanation helps no one, least of all those who say they want real accountability.

Art, as a representation of the last thing humans can be better at than machines, will become more valuable than ever before. 

Neil Gaiman’s advice to graduating students seems more apt than when he gave the speech originally: 

“Life is sometimes hard. Things go wrong, in life and in love and in business and in friendship and in health and in all the other ways that life can go wrong. And when things get tough, this is what you should do.

Make good art.

I’m serious. Husband runs off with a politician? Make good art. Leg crushed and then eaten by mutated boa constrictor? Make good art. IRS on your trail? Make good art. Cat exploded? Make good art. Somebody on the Internet thinks what you do is stupid or evil or it’s all been done before? Make good art. […]

The old rules are crumbling and nobody knows what the new rules are.

So make up your own rules.

Someone asked me recently how to do something she thought was going to be difficult, in this case recording an audio book, and I suggested she pretend that she was someone who could do it. Not pretend to do it, but pretend she was someone who could. She put up a notice to this effect on the studio wall, and she said it helped.

So be wise, because the world needs more wisdom, and if you cannot be wise, pretend to be someone who is wise, and then just behave like they would.

And now go, and make interesting mistakes, make amazing mistakes, make glorious and fantastic mistakes. Break rules. Leave the world more interesting for your being here.

Weekly KAOS - The Vanishing Bond Floor, the Jobs Miss, and the Hormuz Spigot

Welcome to the Weekly KAOS — UrbanKaoboy’s end-of-week roundup covering Macro and Geopolitics, where I try and tease out the most impactful bits of the week.

Themes of the Week
The long end ripped to levels last seen before the Global Financial Crisis and the S&P still printed a record, because with the Bond Floor gone the only thing holding the longest-duration names over the canyon is Growth, while a soft jobs print kept Goldilocks on its feet, Oil stayed two-sided, and China pressed on every front at once.

Anyone who grew up on Saturday-morning cartoons knows the moment: Wile E. Coyote sprints off the edge of the mesa, legs still churning, and stays aloft right up until the instant he looks down. That is exactly how the longest-duration corners of this Equity market feel to me as the 30-year grinds toward yields it last touched in 2002 and the 10-year pushes past 5.2 percent, which is the whole argument of the piece I put out last week, Wile E. Coyote Equities and the Vanishing Bond Floor.

The backup in long rates has quietly pulled the implicit Bond Floor out from under valuations, and the only thing keeping the Mag-7 complex suspended over the canyon is the Growth story.

Meanwhile, our untrusty seismograph needle kept jumping all week, with Bessent conceding to the Bond market that the house does not always win, French and Japanese yields punching through multi-decade highs alongside ours, and the S&P closing green at a record on breadth so narrow that the top four names now outweigh the entire Russell 2000.

I keep coming back to the read I have held since last December: this is the Debt Governor at work, the AI Buildout saturating the capital markets with paper and competing ferociously for capital, not a Fiscal reckoning finally arriving.

Friday's jobs miss then did Warsh a favor even as the FOMC minutes and Waller leaned the other way, while Oil refused to break either way and China kept probing.

Why is the White House holding a hearing on Fed governor Lisa Cook now? Trump explained why in July. 

After the Supreme Court let Cook keep her seat while she challenges his attempt to fire her, Trump said on CNBC that the court "sent it back, not based on the merits. They sent it back on process and procedure." 

"So we'll start the process, and we'll do perfect process and perfect procedure," he said. 

The White House memo made public on Friday *is* that process. It sets a Nov. 5 closed-door hearing at the White House where Justice Department lawyers can question her in front of a three-member committee of Trump appointees about allegations that have yet to result in any criminal charges. The committee then recommends whether there's "cause" to remove her. 

The timing is important here because the day after the White House hearing, Cook and the DOJ owe U,S. District Judge Jia Cobb a joint proposal on how her lawsuit challenging Trump's August 2025 removal effort should proceed. Cobb blocked this removal attempt last year, allowing Cook to remain on the job before the underlying dispute was adjudicated. The Supreme Court upheld that order. The underlying dispute now goes back to her. 

If the committee recommends removal, Trump could fire Cook again, and DOJ would argue she has now had the chance to respond that the Supreme Court and others found lacking. Cobb, and likely the appeals courts after her, would then have to decide whether "cause" had been established. The hearing could also give the administration new material to justify a removal. Even if nothing comes of it, the spectacle of a sitting Fed governor summoned to the White House for questioning sends a message to other officials the president may not be able to fire.

After a wondrous first half for investors, especially for those in growth stocks, the second half of 2026 has been a struggle.  The Russell 3,000 -- which represents roughly 98% of publicly traded US stock market cap -- is up about 3% in the 2nd half, but the average stock in the index is actually down 4.4%.

Along with rising interest rates hurting the most interest-rate sensitive areas of the market, it appears as if the shorts are betting big and winning these days.

We broke the Russell 3,000 into deciles (10 groups of roughly 300 stocks each) based on each stock's short interest as a percentage of its equity float.  We then calculated the average 2nd half percentage change of the stocks in each decile.

Decile one in the chart below all the way to the left of the image, contains the decile of most heavily shorted stocks in the Russell 3,000.  Stocks in this decile are down an average of 13.6% in the 2nd half.  As short interest levels get smaller, performance gets better, and the two deciles containing the least heavily shorted stocks are actually averaging gains in the 2nd half.

During big market rallies, shorts feel the pain and usually push prices higher as they rush to cover.  We're definitely not in that type of environment now, and we haven't been for months.

On the flip side, as the shorts get more confident from their winning ways, the spring gets coiled further.  The next time we get a positive market development that brings investors back into equities, be it from lower oil prices, lower rates, upside earnings, economic surprises, or something that's not on anyone's radar right now, the ensuing short covering could be more extreme than usual.

For now, though, the shorts are winning big in the second half.

Contrary to what many on X believe, I am not a $TSLA hater.  From 2019-2023, $TSLA was my largest position.  In investing, valuation vs price has to matter and if you’re not regularly calculating the difference, you’re not a serious investor. My issue with $TSLA now is that price seems high relative to my estimate of value, so I either wait for future earnings and cash flows to move higher (they are declining right now - see below), or for the stock price to move lower to become attractive again.  

$TSLA stock has significantly underperformed NDX over the past 1, 3, and 5 years, as 2026-2030 earnings estimates have declined, as automation has become a commodity, and as valuation became stretched.  So no, I’m not a TSLA hater;  I just don’t care for the current price relative to my estimate of value.

WHY $TE COULD BE THE NEXT AI POWER MULTIBAGGER

The reason I think T1 could become one of the more asymmetric multi bagger opportunities inside the AI buildout is that the market is still valuing it like a loss making solar manufacturer today while the real thesis is what happens once G2_Austin comes online and turns the company into a much more vertically integrated U.S. power infrastructure supplier. 

G1_Dallas is already showing that the operating model can scale, with Q2 revenue nearly doubling to roughly $250M and gross margin improving toward 20% but G2 is the step change because producing cells internally instead of buying them from outside suppliers should let T1 capture much more of the economics on every module it sells. 

Management believes the initial 2.1 GW phase can eventually support roughly $375M to $450M of annualized adjusted EBITDA and a full 5 GW buildout could push that toward $650M to $700M which is a completely different earnings profile than the company investors are looking at today.

What makes that opportunity much more interesting is that the demand side is increasingly being pulled by the same AI power problem driving the rest of my energy thesis. 

Data centers need enormous amounts of new electricity and solar will not solve that problem alone, but it can become one of the fastest generation sources to deploy when paired with storage, gas and nuclear, especially in markets like ERCOT where interconnection requests are exploding and a huge percentage of the incremental load is tied to data centers. 

T1 already has several gigawatts of contracted module demand through customers like Clearway and Treaty Oak, while its domestic content strategy becomes more valuable as utilities and developers increasingly want U.S. sourced equipment that qualifies for incentives and avoids dependence on Chinese supply chains. 

If G2 works, T1 is not simply selling another commodity solar module because it can own more of the U.S. supply chain from polysilicon and wafers through cells and finished modules, which should create a better margin structure than the current business.

The valuation is where the setup starts becoming interesting because at roughly $4 to $5 per share the market is effectively making investors pay very little for the possibility that G2 actually reaches the profitability management is targeting since consensus around $0.44 of EPS in 2028 puts the stock near roughly 10x those earnings today, which is not demanding if T1 is still growing strongly beyond 2028 and G2 proves that vertically integrated domestic solar can generate sustainable margins. 

The additional optionality around Nordic data centers and battery storage makes the story even broader because T1 could eventually participate not only in supplying generation equipment to the AI buildout but also in owning pieces of the infrastructure around it which is why I think ceiling can be much higher than what a simple solar peer multiple suggests.

The risk is that none of this value exists for shareholders unless the company can actually finance the bridge between today and that future because G2 Phase 1 is expected to cost roughly $510M while unrestricted cash was only around $79M at the end of Q2, so additional debt, equity or both will almost certainly be needed before the factory reaches scale. 

That means dilution and balance sheet risk are very real, and if G2 runs over budget, ramps slowly or fails to reach the expected margin structure then the stock can stay cheap for a good reason.

But if T1 can secure financing without overwhelming existing shareholders, keep G1 margins around or above 20%, bring G2 online in 2027 and convert strong domestic demand into real free cash flow then I think the market could eventually stop viewing T1 as a speculative solar manufacturer and start valuing it as a vertically integrated U.S. power infrastructure platform sitting directly in the path of the AI electricity buildout.
